channel.title: BioFarmLab — Knowledge
channel.description: Knowledge about soil biology, compost and regenerative agriculture.

item.title: How can soil fertility be restored? Compost and the return of life
item.description: How compost helps restore depleted soil, improve its structure and retain water. Regeneration, changes in the soil profile and land quality.

item.title: Biological compost testing: the life you bring to your soil
item.description: What a microscopic compost assessment reveals about bacteria, fungi, protozoa and nematodes in homemade or purchased compost.

item.title: A compost turner for a small tractor: prepare the whole setup
item.description: Choosing a turner for a small tractor means checking drive, slow travel, windrow dimensions and access. What to prepare before discussing a machine.

item.title: Farm composting: from raw material to finished compost
item.description: Organising manure and large windrows: receiving material, composting, maturation and application. Where turners and spreaders fit into the work.

item.title: Turning compost on the farm: the decision starts inside the pile
item.description: Why turn a large compost windrow, and what determines the timing? Temperature, moisture and material structure help guide the decision.

item.title: When is compost ready to use?
item.description: How to recognise mature compost: stable temperature, an earthy smell, crumbly texture and a microscopic assessment of its biology.

item.title: A practical soil biology course: from observation to your own plan
item.description: Assess your soil, make compost and plan regeneration. How practical soil biology helps guide decisions in a garden or on a farm.

item.title: Finished compost: how to use it in gardens and on farms
item.description: Where and when to apply finished compost: beds, orchards and larger crops. How mulch, compost extract and spreading equipment support soil regeneration.

item.title: What happens to manure after 3, 7 and 21 days of composting?
item.description: BioFarmLab documented the transformation of strong-smelling stable manure: its odour and biology changed within days, and observations continued to day 21.

item.title: Chemical vs. biological soil testing: what does each one tell you?
item.description: Chemical testing measures pH and selected nutrients. Microscopy-based biological assessment shows the presence and proportions of major organism groups. The two methods answer different questions.

item.title: Why bottled microbes cannot rebuild degraded soil on their own
item.description: An inoculant can increase selected microorganisms, but cannot by itself recreate their habitat or the entire soil food web.

item.title: Can fertilizer replace soil biology?
item.description: Fertilizer can supply nutrients, but it does not replace decomposition, nutrient cycling, root–microbe interactions or the biological contribution to soil structure.

item.title: A compost turner: turning hours of work into minutes
item.description: Why use a compost turner? A machine that makes turning large windrows, composting horse manure and producing compost on the farm easier.

item.title: Soil or compost problem? Find the cause before you add another product
item.description: Field observation, chemistry, biological assessment and compost process signals provide different information. Start with the question you need answered.

item.title: Why is my compost pile not heating up?
item.description: A compost pile stays cool when microbial activity is limited or when the heat being produced escapes too quickly. The same symptom can have several causes.

item.title: Restoring soil biology: what are we rebuilding?
item.description: Restoring soil biology means rebuilding nutrient cycling, organic matter breakdown, soil structure and relationships between roots and soil organisms.

item.title: How to collect soil, compost and liquid samples for biological testing
item.description: A sample should represent the material or place you want to assess. Collection differs for soil, compost and liquids.

item.title: Kiss the Ground: a starting point, not a handbook
item.description: Kiss the Ground shows why soil matters for farming, water and the carbon cycle. Treat it as an introduction, not scientific proof or a ready-made method.

item.title: What is the soil food web?
item.description: The soil food web consists of soil organisms and the flow of energy and matter between them, from bacteria and fungi to protists, nematodes and larger animals.

item.title: Does the countryside have to smell? What manure odour tells us
item.description: Fresh manure has an odour, but a strong rotten smell is not inevitable. Ammonia, hydrogen sulphide and other volatile compounds reveal what is happening in the material.

item.title: Where do plants get nutrients? Roots are only part of the system
item.description: Plants absorb water and mineral ions through roots. Soil biology influences how nutrients change, circulate and become available.
